newsitem.title: USA: NY Bruno says end NYC rent rules, Giuliani says no.
newsitem.headline: NY Bruno says end NYC rent rules, Giuliani says no.

text.p: The Republican-led New York State Senate on Thursday proposed ending New York City's rent rules, but Democratic lawmakers and Mayor Rudolph Giuliani quickly said they oppposed the plan.
Gov. George Pataki, who said he supported moving the city to a market system, offered few details about how this would be accomplished.
"The Rent Control system needs a strong dose of common sense and I hope we can reach a consensus on reforms," Pataki said, in prepared remarks.

Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno (R-Troy), in a speech given to the Rent Stabilization Association in the city, called for ending "Rent regulation as we know it," arguing that this was the best way to create a competitive housing market and promote new construction.

He cited a study by the Manhattan Policy Research Institute that said the city needs to add 20,000 apartments a year just to keep up with its rising population, and 40,000 units a year to improve housing and cut prices. In a "good year," the city loses 14,000 to 19,000 apartments a year, he added.

The impact of abolishing the rent rules, which include ones that set rates for rent-stabilized and rent-controlled apartments, would not be felt for two years after the current regulations expire on June 15, 1997.

And Bruno proposed cushioning the impact on the city's most vulnerable citizens by continuing the program for senior and disabled citizens and perhaps expanding it to low-income seniors. Pataki also said he supported continuing protections for senior and disabled citizens and those on fixed incomes.

A spokesman for the House Speaker, Sheldon Silver (D-Manhattan), who saw the city's loft laws used against him during the protracted battle over the 1997 fiscal year budget, referred calls to Vito Lopez (D-Brooklyn).

Lopez emphasized the issue's importance and all but ruled out abolishing the current system. "This will be one of our top issues, and I believe as in any other process we've been through, we're not going to walk out and eliminate rent protections in New York City."

Giuliani, a Republican, also reacted coldly to the proposal by the Senate Majority Leader. "I support rent regulation. I think we have struck a reasonable balance in New York City with our rent regulations and our rent increases," he said, in a statement released by a spokeswoman. The mayor added that both tenants and landlords have at times blasted the current regime.
"That's something we have to live with, and it works out pretty well," he said.
